title: How CRISPR-Cas9 edits genomes with precision
dek: How a bacterial immune defense was repurposed into a programmable molecular scissor.
sentences: Bacteria have evolved sophisticated immune defenses to protect themselves from invading viral bacteriophages.
The most versatile of these mechanisms is CRISPR-Cas9, an adaptive system that stores fragments of past viral attackers.
When a known virus attacks again, the bacterium transcribes a matching piece of guide RNA.
This guide RNA forms a complex with the Cas9 enzyme and navigates the cell to locate the complementary target DNA sequence.
Once the target match is verified, Cas9 acts as molecular scissors, cutting both strands of the target DNA double helix.
The host cell detects this double-strand break as an emergency and initiates internal repair mechanisms.
In natural repair, the cell frequently glues the broken ends together imperfectly, disabling the targeted gene entirely.
Alternatively, scientists can provide a synthetic DNA template alongside the Cas9 complex.
The cell's repair machinery then uses this template to write a brand new sequence directly into the damaged region.
CRISPR does not create the new genetic material by itself; it simply cuts DNA and lets natural cellular repair systems do the rebuilding.
This modular mechanism has revolutionized biological research by turning complex genetic editing into a predictable programmable process.

keyPoints.statement: Guide RNA directs the Cas9 enzyme to a complementary DNA sequence where Cas9 cuts both strands.
keyPoints.addHint: Explain how Cas9 targets DNA: guide RNA leads the Cas9 enzyme to a matching sequence and Cas9 cuts both strands.

keyPoints.statement: CRISPR does not synthesize new DNA itself; it only cuts, leaving the rebuilding to host repair enzymes.

commonMisconceptions.statement: CRISPR creates and writes new genes completely by itself
commonMisconceptions.why: The article explains that CRISPR only cuts DNA; host repair mechanisms do the actual rebuilding.
commonMisconceptions.correction: CRISPR acts as a molecular scissor that cuts DNA; it relies on natural cellular repair mechanisms to insert or rebuild sequences.
any: creates new dna on its own

commonMisconceptions.statement: Cas9 searches and cuts DNA sequences at random
commonMisconceptions.why: Cas9 is guided specifically by complementary guide RNA to an exact match.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Cas9 does not cut randomly; it is guided to a precise target sequence by a complementary guide RNA molecule.

samples.label: Clear explanation
samples.text: The article describes how CRISPR-Cas9 edits genomes with high precision. Bacteria evolved this system to defend against viruses. Guide RNA directs the Cas9 enzyme to a matching target DNA sequence, where Cas9 cuts both strands of the double helix. The cell senses this break and activates its repair machinery. If left alone, imperfect repair often disables the gene; if scientists supply a synthetic DNA template, the cell incorporates the new sequence. CRISPR does not create new DNA itself; it only makes the cut and lets cellular repair do the rewriting.

samples.label: Contains a misconception
samples.text: CRISPR-Cas9 is a technology that creates genes by itself. The Cas9 enzyme floats through the cell and randomly cuts DNA until it finds a good spot to insert synthetic DNA. Once it finds a spot it writes the whole gene directly without needing the cell's repair systems. This makes genetic editing fast and easy for scientists.
